> “Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while, ˹for˺ you are truly wicked.”

The sūrah steps back into the world, and its voice turns to iron: *kulū wa-tamattaʿū qalīlan, innakum mujrimūn* — eat, take your enjoyment, a little while; you are, in truth, criminals. The command-form here is the classical *āmru t-tasallī wa-t-tahakkum* — the imperative of scorn and of handing-over, the same grammar as the Fire's *go on to what you used to deny* (77:29 — *“˹The disbelievers will be told,˺ “Proceed into that ˹Fire˺ which you used to deny”*).

*Tamattaʿū*: extract the benefit, enjoy the use — the word for grazing, for taking usufruct of a thing.

**Qalīlan: The Whole World Measured as a Mouthful**

The timeframe-word is the sentence's true violence. *Qalīlan* — a little — reduces all their decades, all their trade seasons and building projects and feasts, to a single diminutive. The Book states the same sentence with the arithmetic written out: *“We allow them enjoyment for a little while, then in time We will force them into a harsh torment”* (31:24) — enjoyment; littleness; force; harshness. The four stations of the respite are the verse's own four words, magnified.

Set beside the Day's clock, the diminutive is precise rather than cruel: the world's whole span, measured at the Day, is *“no more than an hour of a day”* (10:45), and even those granted the longest enjoyment confirm at the end that *“an hour”* is what it amounted to (46:35 — *“On the Day they see what they have been threatened with, it will be as if they had only stayed ˹in this world˺ for an hour of a day.”*). *Qalīlan* is not God's belittling rhetoric but the proportion finally published — the correct unit of measure for the thing they were calling *life*.

**Istidrāj: The Respite Named Elsewhere**

The Book has a doctrine-word for this terrifying arrangement, *istidrāj* — the stepwise drawing-on: *“So leave to Me ˹O Prophet˺ those who reject this message. We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot understand. I ˹only˺ delay their end for a while, but My planning is compelling”* (68:44-45). Delay, here, is not acquittal; it is the plan. God's patience is structured, purposeive, and ends at a scheduled station the enjoyers cannot see.

**The Two Imperatives of Eating, Set Side by Side**

Three verses apart, the sūrah has now lodged the same verb at both tables: *kulū wa-shrabū hanīʾan bimā kuntum taʿmalūn* for the beautiful-doers (77:43 — *“˹They will be told,˺ “Eat and drink happily for what you used to do.”*), *kulū wa-tamattaʿū qalīlan* for the criminals. Every difference is a doctrine. Drink is dropped from the second address — the welcome's fullness, contracted. *Hanīʾan*, wholesomely without consequence, is replaced by *qalīlan* — with nothing but consequence ahead. And the causal clauses invert: *for what you used to do* honours the dinner; *you are truly wicked* indicts the diner.

Food becomes, at the sūrah's close, its final test-case of the provision-theology. Under the oath (77:25-27 — *“Have We not made the earth a lodging for the living and the dead and placed upon it towering, firm mountains, and given you fresh water to drink”*) provision asked one question — will you be grateful or deny? — and the two imperative-verses publish the two answers' destinations: the grateful hear *eat — wholesome, without end*; the deniers hear *eat — brief, with the verdict attached*. The same mouths, the same verb, opposite eternities. Nothing in the Book's moral physics is plainer than that contrast, drawn in a single verb of hospitality.

**The Ninth Toll, Over the Little While**

The bell rises for its ninth full toll, directly above the respite-address. *Waylun yawmaʾidhin lil-mukadhdhibīn*. Context decides the shaft: the immediately preceding exhibit was the wicked *eating and enjoying* on a little-while licence, their enjoyment labelled and their file sealed. The ninth woe, say the close readers of this station, hangs over those whose enjoyment-blindness was itself a practice of denial — the ones who lived as though the respite were the estate.

The toll arrests a specific spiritual obtuseness, sharper than the doctrinal denials rung earlier. A person may never dispute a creed aloud and still practice atheism with both hands: eating, gathering, enjoying, with never a thought that the table has an Owner and the meal a term. The Book names that condition — drawing near of judgment while the heedless turn away is its standing portrait of the age: *“˹The time of˺ people's judgment has drawn near, yet they are heedlessly turning away”* (21:1). Nearness, here; turning-away, there: the ninth toll stands over exactly that geometry.

**God Keeps the Receipts of Good Meals**

Nothing in the verse lightens enjoyment itself; what makes the respite damnable is enjoyment *unquestioned*. The Book is explicit that the meal will be examined: *“Then, on that Day, you will definitely be questioned about ˹your worldly˺ pleasures”* (102:8). The pleasures — *an-naʿīm*, the soft goods of ease — are not neutral items; they are audit-items, every one receipted, the whole table called into the account.

The question lodged against the wicked is therefore not *did you enjoy?* but *did enjoyment conclude in gratitude or in denial?* — the same fork the oath hung over the receptacle, the anchors and the sweet water (77:25-27 — *“Have We not made the earth a lodging for the living and the dead and placed upon it towering, firm mountains, and given you fresh water to drink”*). The guilty of 77:46-47 — *“Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while, ˹for˺ you are truly wicked.”* are those who answered every gift with the extension of appetite only, whose feasts never forwarded a single thought upward. God's grievance here is not pleasure but perpetuity-pretense: the feast enrolled as a worldview, the little while styled as the long estate.

The pattern of the final pair is already visible: enjoyment received wrongly (46-47) and worship refused completely (48-49) — consumption and devotion, the two poles of a human day.

**The Day Separates the Eaters by Their Thanks**

Set the two tables against each other one last time. At the garden-table, enjoyment is issued *for what you used to do*, and the diners' whole history of gratitude is quoted back to them in the causal clause (77:43 — *“˹They will be told,˺ “Eat and drink happily for what you used to do.”*). At the respite-table, enjoyment is issued *a little*, and the diners' whole history of heedlessness is quoted in the verdict that follows. The separation at the Day is nothing but the crystalization, at last, of each table's daily customs.

Neither table is reached by accident. The practices were free; the answers were daily; the audit ran silently all the while (36:54 awaiting only its hour — *“On that Day no soul will be wronged in the least, nor will you be rewarded except for what you used to do”*). The ninth toll rings over the class precisely because no other headline could fit: those who made a creed out of their appetite — who treated the delay as the promise — have nothing ahead of them to greet but the very Day whose whole atmosphere their enjoyment refused to admit. Meanwhile the drinks themselves bear the moral key: the Fire's cup scalds what it touches, the garden's cup never harms (37:46-47 — *“It will neither harm ˹them˺, nor will they be intoxicated by it”*) — two liquids for two lifetimes of answer.

**The Majority Reading: This Is the Call to Prayer**

The dominant interpretation among the commentators identifies the bow with the ṣalāh itself — *r-kaʿū* as the command's shorthand for *pray*, since the bow is the prayer's indispensable, defining movement, the one repeated in every unit of it. On this reading the verse is a verdict on those who were summoned to the central act of worship every day of their lives and never once entered it. Some of the earliest local readers even placed this verse in Medina, where the congregational call gave the command its institutional form — a note preserved to explain the verse's address-style against the sūrah's Meccan scenery.

The prayer-command reading also fits the sūrah's internal logic with precision. The oaths concerned the delivered-word; the world's exhibits concerned how that word was answered — by ungrateful consumption (77:46 — *“Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while, ˹for˺ you are truly wicked.”*) and here by unprayed prayer. Worship, in Islam's account of it, is the reminder's first address to the limbs: *“Establish prayer, pay alms-tax. Bow down with those who bow down”* (2:43) — the same bow, standing in the believer's own charter, commanded in the company-imperative that makes refusal not merely lonely but communal treason: they would not bow *with the bowers*.

**The Second Reading: The Call That Comes on the Day**

A second strand reads the command about the Last Dayly: bowing will one day be commanded where refusal is no longer available as a real option, and the refusal's final form will be *inability*. The verse that sustains this reading is among the most terrible in the Book: *“˹Beware of˺ the Day the Shin ˹of Allah˺ will be bared, and the wicked will be asked to prostrate, but they will not be able to do so, with eyes downcast, totally humbled. For they were always called to prostrate ˹in the world˺ when they were fully capable ˹but they chose not to˺”* (68:42-43).

On this reading, 77:48 — *“When it is said to them, “Bow down ˹before Allah,” they do not bow”* is that Day's exhibit of origins: the record is produced of the *world's* calls — when it was said to them, bow — and the sustained refusal is read as the reason for the back's new condition. Called when capable, incapable when compelled: the symmetry is naked justice. Capability was the gift; refusal spent it; the Day collects what the refusal made permanent. Whether the verse speaks of the world's command with the Day's echo behind it, or of the Day's command explained by the world's record, the two readings preach one stripped back of alternatives: they would not, so they will not be able to; the posture refused freely becomes the posture impossible.

**A Whole Creed in One Movement of the Spine**

The Book has tracked this bone-allegiance since its opening pages: when the first command of prostration was issued in the angelic assembly, one refused *“and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful”* (2:34), and the classical observers have noted ever since that pride's native seat is the spine. The servants of the Compassionate are drawn by the opposite silhouette: *“those who spend the night prostrating themselves before their Lord and standing ˹in prayer˺”* (25:63-64). Night after night, the two humanities are sketched in dark clothing: some curved toward their Lord in the dark, some stood straight over their beds of heedlessness. 77:48 — *“When it is said to them, “Bow down ˹before Allah,” they do not bow”* simply weighs the two postures in the balance of the Day.

**The Final Toll Hangs Over the Unbowed**

The choice of terminal station is itself the lesson. Every earlier toll mounted a *scene* of the Day or the world-past; the tenth mounts a *refusal* — a thing not done, a negative space. Woe, at its most surgical, attaches not to crimes of commission here but to abstention: they did not bow. God's last word of woe in this sūrah reserves its weight for the easiest obedience declined, for faith's minimal physical courtesy, dispensed with.

**Ten Tollings: The Design Becomes Visible Whole**

**Denial's Last Mask Is Liturgical**

**The Ten Warnings and Where This One Falls**

This is the last of the sūrah's ten warnings, and the behaviour it hangs over is the refusal of the simplest act of worship. The people it addresses are the ones who were told to bow and did not bow (77:48 describes them — *“When it is said to them, “Bow down ˹before Allah,” they do not bow”*). So the last warning in the sūrah lands not on some enormous crime but on a prayer-mat that went unused (77:49 is the verse — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*).

The earlier warnings are spread through the sūrah. One falls at the first mention of the Day (77:15 states it — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*). Then over the lessons of history that went unheeded (77:19 describes it — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*). Then over a person's denial of his own origins (77:24 states it — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*). Then over ungrateful use of what was provided (77:28 describes it — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*). Then over the fire that people are marched to (77:34 describes it — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*). Then over the voice that is taken away (77:37 states it — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*). Then over the gathering of all generations (77:40 describes it — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*). Then over the garden that was forfeited (77:45 states it — *“˹But˺ woe on that Day to the deniers”*). Then over the time that was given and spent anyway (77:47 describes it — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*). And last, over the spine that would not bend (77:49 is the verse — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*).

No other sūrah in the Book repeats a single sentence of this kind ten times. The nearest echo comes once, in another sūrah of the same period (83:10 states it — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*). So the repetition is a design rather than a habit. A hearer who follows the sūrah to its close hears the same sentence ten times, and that is how a line stays in the memory and starts repeating itself when the person is alone.

The last two warnings before this one fall on pleasure and then on worship (77:47 describes the first — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers”*). The order carries a message of its own, since a person's denial can hide either in open rejection or in religious language that never reaches the body.

> So what message after this ˹Quran˺ would they believe in

**The Sūrah Ends by Asking**

The fiftieth verse closes the sūrah not with a verdict but with a question: *fa-bi-ayyi ḥadīthin baʿdahū yuʾminūn* — in what discourse, then, after it, will they believe? Grammar does the whole work. *Fa-*: so, then — the connector of exhausted argument, the word a speaker uses when every exhibit is in and the conclusion is owed. *Bi-ayyi ḥadīthin*: with whatever word, discourse, account. *Baʿdahū*: after it — after *this*, the recitation just concluded. *Yuʾminūn*: will they believe — future-directed, still open.

A sūrah that began by swearing upon winds ends by interrogating its own audience.

This closing query belongs to a small, prestigious family in the Book. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf ends a long review of creation, providence and squandered time with the identical sentence: *“Have they ever reflected on the wonders of the heavens and the earth, and everything Allah has created, and that perhaps their end is near? So what message after this ˹Quran˺ would they believe in?”* (7:185). Sūrah al-Jāthiyah runs the same form with its terms tightened: *“These are Allah's revelations which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth. So what message will they believe in after ˹denying˺ Allah and His revelations?”* (45:6).

**After This: The Dead End of the Demand for More**

The hinge of the question is the phrase *after it*. It does not ask whether *some* message might convince them elsewhere; it asks what could possibly remain in the category *message* once *this* one has been declined. The sūrah itself has just itemized what kind of ḥadīth this is: an address witnessed by winds and angels (77:1-5 — *“By those ˹winds˺ sent forth successively and those blowing violently and those scattering ˹rainclouds˺ widely And ˹by˺ those ˹angels˺ fully distinguishing ˹truth from falsehood˺ and those delivering revelation”*), docketed with the record of the ancient nations (77:16-18 — *“Did We not destroy earlier disbelievers And We will make the later disbelievers follow them This is how We deal with the wicked”*), anatomized inside the hearer's own embryo (77:20-23 — *“Did We not create you from a humble fluid placing it in a secure place until an appointed time We ˹perfectly˺ ordained ˹its development˺. How excellent are We in doing so”*), argued from his water and his mountains (77:25-27 — *“and placed upon it towering, firm mountains, and given you fresh water to drink”*).

Projected across both doors of the Last Day in furnished detail (77:28-44 — *“Woe on that Day to the deniers ˹The disbelievers will be told,˺ “Proceed into that ˹Fire˺ which you used to deny Proceed into the shade ˹of smoke˺ which rises in three columns providing neither coolness nor shelter from the flames Indeed, it hurls sparks ˹as big˺ as huge castles and ˹as dark˺ as black camels.” Woe on that Day to the deniers On that Day they will not ˹be in a position to˺ speak nor will they be permitted to offer excuses”*). If a hearer leaves all of that unmoved, the Book's verdict is: the defect is not in the supply of messages.

This is also why the Qur'an treats further-demanded proofs with such dry patience elsewhere: *“So leave to Me ˹O Prophet˺ those who reject this message. We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot understand”* (68:44). Leave them to Me — the demand for a different message receives no new message; it receives a sentence. The question of 77:50 — *“So what message after this ˹Quran˺ would they believe in”* is so not a promise of more evidence, nor a concession that better evidence exists; it is the formal exposure that the demand for *more* was never an account of knowledge but a therapy for the will.

**What, Concretely, Could Follow This One?**

Take the options seriously for a moment, as the question invites. Another book? It would either match this one's message — in which case rejecting it reduplicates the refusal, as the Qur'an repeatedly observes of disputes among scripture-holders — or contradict it, forfeiting the very signature of the same God. Another prophet? The prophets have been coming for ages; the sūrah at its start delivered the record of what happened to those whose pattern-fit was denied (77:16-18 — *“Did We not destroy earlier disbelievers And We will make the later disbelievers follow them This is how We deal with the wicked”*). Spectacle-miracles on demand? The Day itself is the promised spectacle, and its very certainty is what the question's audience is busily deferring. *Signs that they pass by with indifference* is the Book's standing observation of that demand: *“How many signs in the heavens and the earth do they pass by with indifference!”* (12:105).
